scenes.script_line: Imagine an area of land that has suffered damage. We could simply stop disturbing it. That may help. But sometimes recovery also needs carefully planned protection, planting or water management. That's the idea of regeneration: not only reducing damage, but helping a living system become healthier. Ask not only, 'What can we avoid?' Ask, 'What can we help recover?'

scenes.script_line: Imagine planting one hundred trees. Have we built a healthy woodland? Not necessarily. Trees need suitable soil, water, other plants and relationships with living organisms. Birds and insects also need habitats. Regeneration isn't a numbers contest. A tree planted is a beginning, not the whole result. The real question is whether the ecosystem grows healthier over time.

scenes.script_line: A building team can complete a wall in days. A young cork oak may need many years to become a mature tree. Different work. Different clocks. That's why the decisions we make today matter so much. We should never assume that damaged nature can be quickly replaced. Some of our most valuable contributions are simply protecting what already exists.

scenes.script_line: A swept workshop floor is excellent. But a natural area without leaves, grass or insects is not automatically healthier. Living landscapes can look untidy to an untrained eye. That's why we have different standards for different places. Keep worksites clean and safe. Leave protected ecological areas under appropriate management. Good care begins by knowing the difference.

scenes.script_line: Imagine returning here in twenty years. The buildings look beautiful. But so do the trees, the soil and the habitats around them. Wouldn't that be a greater achievement than buildings alone? Regeneration invites us to think about the whole place. Not just what we construct. Also what can thrive because we worked carefully. Leave more life behind.
